hints: Form the displacement vectors using endpoint minus start point: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{CD}=\overrightarrow{OD}-\overrightarrow{OC}\).
Calculate each length with \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\), keeping the square roots exact.
Compare the squared components and simplify the radicals to verify the factor of 2 between \(AB\) and \(CD\).
Apply \(\cos\theta=(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CD})/(|AB||CD|)\), retaining the sign of the scalar product because the directions are specified.
Evaluate the inverse cosine in a consistent angular unit; do not replace the resulting obtuse directed angle by its supplement.

State the vectors representing the directions of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD}$:
$$\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \overrightarrow{CD} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Recall the magnitudes found in part (a):
$$|\overrightarrow{AB}| = 2\sqrt{6}, \quad |\overrightarrow{CD}| = \sqrt{6}$$

State the angle rounded to $1$ decimal place (or $2$ decimal places in radians):

hints: Write the two lines as \(\mathbf r=(2,1,5)+\lambda(2,-2,-4)\) and \(\mathbf r=(1,1,2)+\mu(2,1,1)\).
If they intersect, corresponding components must be equal for the same pair \((\lambda,\mu)\); solve any two component equations.
Substitute those parameter values into the remaining component equation and exhibit the contradiction, then conclude that no intersection exists.
walkthrough:
Write the vector equations of the line through $A, B$ and the line through $C, D$:
Line $AB$ with parameter $\lambda$:
$$\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$$
Line $CD$ with parameter $\mu$:
$$\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

Equate corresponding components to set up three equations for a point of intersection:
$$2 + 2\lambda = 1 + 2\mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 1, } x\text{-component)}$$
$$1 - 2\lambda = 1 + \mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 2, } y\text{-component)}$$
$$5 - 4\lambda = 2 + \mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 3, } z\text{-component)}$$

Substitute $\lambda = -\dfrac{1}{6}$ and $\mu = \dfrac{1}{3}$ into Equation 3 to test consistency:
$$\text{LHS} = 5 - 4\left(-\dfrac{1}{6}\right) = 5 + \dfrac{4}{6} = 5 + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{17}{3}$$
$$\text{RHS} = 2 + \mu = 2 + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{7}{3}$$
Conclude that because the system of equations is inconsistent, there is no common point, and therefore the line through $A$ and $B$ does not intersect the line through $C$ and $D$.
